focus.text: A conditional sentence has two parts: an if clause that sets a condition, and a main clause that gives the result. The verb forms you choose tell the reader whether you think the condition is likely, unlikely or impossible. Real conditionals describe things that do happen or easily could happen; hypothetical conditionals describe a situation you have only imagined. The if clause never takes will or would, however far into the future it looks. Either half can come first, and when the if clause comes first it takes a comma.

summaryTable.caption: The four patterns at a glance
rows: If the bus **is** late, I **will walk**.
If I **had** more time, I **would join** the club.
If I **had revised**, I **would have passed**.

pretest.sentence: If the shop closes early, we buy our lunch at the market.
pretest.reason: A situation that repeats takes the present simple in both clauses.

pretest.sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
pretest.reason: The *if* clause takes the present: *If it rains tomorrow*.

pretest.sentence: If you hand the form in late, the office will not accept it.
pretest.reason: A likely future condition takes the present simple plus *will*.

pretest.sentence: If I see Nga tomorrow, I tell her about the meeting.
pretest.reason: One future result needs *will*: *I will tell her about the meeting*.

pretest.sentence: Water freezes if the temperature falls below zero.
pretest.reason: A fact that is always true takes the present in both clauses, and no comma is needed here.

pretest.sentence: If the library is full, we will to study at home.
pretest.reason: A modal is followed by the base verb: *we will study*.

pretest.sentence: If I lived closer to the campus, I would cycle every day.
pretest.reason: An unreal present situation takes the past simple after *if* and *would* + base verb.

pretest.sentence: If she studied harder last year, she would pass the entrance exam.
pretest.reason: For an unreal past, use *had studied* and *would have passed*.

pretest.sentence: If Khoa had taken the earlier bus, he would not be waiting now.
pretest.reason: A mixed conditional: an unreal past cause (*had taken*) with a result that is true now.

pretest.sentence: Unless you don't submit the essay by Friday, you will lose marks.
pretest.reason: *Unless* already means *if not*, so the second negative reverses the meaning.

context.title: Planning the clean-up day
context.paragraph: Our class is planning a clean-up day at the riverside park next month. If the weather is dry, we will start at seven in the morning. If it rains heavily, we will move the whole event to the following Saturday. Unless every group brings its own gloves, the teachers cannot let us collect broken glass. Nga says that if she had known about the project earlier, she would have asked her uncle to lend us a van. Provided that the council approves our plan, a lorry will take the rubbish away at noon. If we finish before lunch, we will get free drinks from the café opposite the gate.
targets: we will start at seven in the morning
Unless every group brings its own gloves
if she had known about the project earlier
she would have asked her uncle to lend us a van
Provided that the council approves our plan

sections.title: Forming real conditionals

table.caption: Real conditionals: the forms
rows: If the tide **goes** out, the boats **rest** on the sand.
If the fee **rises**, fewer students **will enrol**.
If you **book** early, you **may get** a discount.
If the alarm **sounds**, **leave** by the back door.

notes: The *if* clause never takes *will*, even when it points to the future: *If the bus is late* — not *if the bus will be late*.
When the *if* clause comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes second, no comma is needed.

items.stem: If the rain ___ before six, we will cycle to the market.
items.reason: The *if* clause takes the present simple, and *the rain* is third person singular.

items.stem: If you leave now, you ___ the last ferry.
items.reason: A likely future result takes *will* plus the base verb.

items.stem: If the temperature ___ above 35 degrees, the school cancels afternoon sport.
items.reason: A rule that is always true takes the present simple in both clauses.

items.stem: If Hùng ___ his wallet at home, he will not be able to pay.
items.reason: The *if* clause stays in the present, however far into the future it looks.

items.stem: If you ___ the instructions carefully, you may avoid the common mistakes.
items.reason: The *if* clause stays in the present simple even when the sentence looks forward, and *you* adds no -s.

sections.title: Using real conditionals

rules.text: Use present plus present when the result always follows: a rule, a habit or a scientific fact.

examples.text: If the canteen **runs** out of rice, it **serves** noodles instead.
If a pupil **misses** three classes, the school **calls** the parents.

rules.text: Use present plus *will* when you are talking about one likely situation in the future.

examples.text: If the council **builds** the new line, my journey **will take** twenty minutes.
We **will postpone** the trip if the forecast **is** bad.

rules.text: Swap *will* for *may*, *might*, *can* or *should* when you want to soften the result, which is useful in academic writing.

examples.text: If sea levels **rise** further, several districts **may flood**.
If the city **charges** for parking, drivers **might use** the bus.

tips: In a Task 2 essay, a first conditional is the cleanest way to argue a consequence: *If the government subsidises train tickets, fewer people will drive into the centre.*

sections.title: Forming hypothetical conditionals

table.caption: Hypothetical and mixed conditionals: the forms
rows: If I **were** you, I **would apply** today.
If she **had asked**, we **would have helped**.
If they **had left** earlier, they **would be** here now.
If he **were** more careful, he **would not have lost** his keys.

notes: The past forms here do not mean past time; they mean that the situation is not real. *If I had a car* is about today, not about yesterday.
*Were* is the formal choice for every subject in a second conditional: *If the report were shorter, more people would read it.* *Was* is common in speech.

items.stem: If I ___ in Đà Nẵng, I would swim every morning before work.
items.reason: An unreal present situation takes the past simple in the *if* clause.

items.stem: If the team had trained harder, they ___ the final.
items.reason: An unreal past result takes *would have* plus the past participle.

items.stem: If Lan had caught the earlier train, she ___ in Huế by now.
items.reason: The cause is in the past but the result is true now, so use *would* plus the base verb.

items.stem: If I ___ the answer, I would tell you straight away.
items.reason: The situation is unreal now, not in the past, so use the past simple.

items.stem: If the school had bought new computers last year, the lab ___ so crowded today.
items.reason: A mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result takes *would* plus the base verb.

sections.title: Using hypothetical and mixed conditionals

rules.text: Use the second conditional for a present or future situation you know is not true, or think is very unlikely.

examples.text: If the city **had** a metro line, the air **would be** cleaner.
If I **were** the head teacher, I **would shorten** the lunch break.

rules.text: Use the third conditional to look back at something that did not happen and imagine a different past.

examples.text: If we **had booked** the hostel earlier, we **would have paid** half the price.
Trang **would have joined** the trip if her passport **had arrived** in time.

rules.text: Mix the two patterns when the condition and the result belong to different times. Keep each half in its own form.

examples.text: If Minh **had chosen** science, he **would be** studying medicine now.
If I **were** better at maths, I **would have taken** the engineering course.

rules.text: Keep *would* in the main clause. An *if* clause takes a past form instead.

examples.text: If the bus **came** more often, I would not need a motorbike.
If they **offered** scholarships, more students would apply.

notes: The one common exception to the last rule is the polite formula *If you would like more information, please contact the office*, which is a request rather than a condition.
tips: Hypothetical conditionals are useful for recommendations: *If schools started later, teenagers would sleep longer.* Follow one with evidence, or it reads as a guess.

items.sentence: If the ferry will leave at six, we need to be at the port by five.
items.reason: The *if* clause takes the present, not *will*.

items.sentence: If I would have more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
items.reason: *Would* belongs in the main clause; the *if* clause takes the past simple.

items.sentence: If she had revised the vocabulary, she would pass the test last Friday.
items.reason: The result is in the past too, so use *would have* plus the past participle.

items.sentence: Unless you don't bring your student card, you will pay the full price.
items.reason: *Unless* already means *if not*, so a second negative reverses the meaning.

items.sentence: If the price fell a little, many more people would to buy electric bikes.
items.reason: A modal is followed by the base verb, never by *to* plus a verb.

sections.title: Using unless, provided that and even if

rules.text: *Unless* means *if not*, so the clause after it stays positive.

examples.text: **Unless the rain stops**, the match will be cancelled.
You cannot enter the lab **unless you wear** closed shoes.

rules.text: Use *provided that*, *as long as* or *on condition that* when the condition is a requirement you are setting.

examples.text: You can borrow my notes **provided that you return them** by Friday.
The club accepts new members **as long as they attend** two sessions a month.

rules.text: Use *even if* when the result does not change, and *in case* for a precaution you take in advance.

examples.text: **Even if the fee doubles**, I will finish the course.
Take a raincoat **in case the weather changes**.

notes: *In case* is not a conditional. *If it rains, I will take an umbrella* is a reaction; *I will take an umbrella in case it rains* is a precaution you take before anything happens.
tips: *Unless* is strong, so it suits rules and warnings. In a balanced essay, *provided that* and *as long as* sound fairer: *Higher fees are acceptable provided that grants exist.*

editing.text: Last term our school ran a free coding course, and I still regret that I did not sign up. If I would have joined it in September, I would know how to build a simple website by now. My friend Khang took the course, and he says that if he had not learned Python, he will not have found his part-time job at a start-up in Đà Nẵng. The teacher told us that if students attend every session, they receive a certificate. Unless you don't miss more than two classes, the certificate is yours. I asked my parents about the fee for the next course. Because I really want to continue. They said that if the price fell a little, they would to pay for it. If the school offer the course again, I will apply on the first day, and when I will start university, I hope to study computer science.

errors.reason: *Would* belongs in the main clause; an unreal past condition takes *had* plus the past participle.
A third conditional takes *would have* plus the past participle, not *will have*.
*Unless* already means *if not*, so *don't* reverses the meaning.
A *because* clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.
A modal is followed by the base verb with no *to*.
*The school* is third person singular, so the verb takes -s.
A future time clause takes the present, not *will*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a classmate who missed the meeting about the school trip. Explain what will happen if the group reaches thirty people, and what will happen if it does not.
checklist: At least three first conditionals: a present form after *if* and *will* in the main clause.
Neither *will* nor *would* appears inside an *if* clause.
A comma follows every *if* clause that comes first.

topics.prompt: Some people say that if public transport were free, city centres would be far cleaner. How far do you agree? Give reasons and an example.
checklist: At least two second conditionals with a past form after *if* and *would* plus the base verb.
At least one result is softened with *might*, *may* or *could*.
*Unless*, *provided that* or *as long as* appears at least once.

topics.prompt: Look back at a decision you made two or three years ago, such as a school, a club or a subject. Describe what happened, then imagine how your life would be different today if you had chosen otherwise.
checklist: At least two third conditionals: *had* plus the past participle, then *would have* plus the past participle.
At least one mixed conditional: an unreal past condition with a result that is true now.
Past forms after *if* describe unreal situations, not past time.
